analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage to $6.50 and ends tax deductions for executive pay over 25 times the lowest worker's wage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour, a jump of more than 50%. It would also have changed the tax code so companies could no longer deduct executive pay that exceeds 25 times what their lowest-paid employee makes. Any pay above that line would still be legal, but the company would pay for it with after-tax dollars instead of getting a taxpayer subsidy for it. The bill never moved after being referred to two House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of minimum-wage workers would have seen their hourly pay rise from $4.25 to as much as $6.50. Taxpayers generally would benefit from no longer subsidizing very high executive pay through deductible business expenses.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $6.50 an hour, effective 90 days after enactment [S2] [S3].
Denies employers a federal tax deduction for any employee's compensation that exceeds 25 times the compensation of the company's lowest-paid full-time employee [S2] [S3].

The tax provision counts only salary, wages, and bonuses as compensation, treats all commonly-controlled businesses as one employer, and annualizes pay for part-year workers to prevent gaming through split employment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wages — especially restaurants, retail, and other low-wage industries — would bear higher payroll costs. Large corporations with very high executive pay would lose a tax break on the amount above the 25-to-1 ratio.

drawbacks.text: A minimum wage increase of this size (roughly 53% at once) would raise labor costs sharply for businesses that rely on low-wage labor, and opponents argued it could cost some entry-level jobs [S2] [S3].
The 25-to-1 ratio counts only salary, wages, and bonuses, so companies could keep deducting other forms of executive pay, such as stock options, by shifting compensation into those forms [S3].

Firms could stay under the ratio by outsourcing or restructuring so their lowest-paid workers are not their own employees, since the rule applies only to compensation paid by a treated-single employer [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage increase would put real money in the pockets of the lowest-paid workers, and the tax change would simply stop taxpayers from helping to underwrite extreme executive pay — the pay itself would not be capped. The honest costs are that a one-time 53% wage floor increase is abrupt for small low-margin employers, and the pay-ratio rule has loopholes around stock compensation and contracting. A phase-in and broader compensation definition would have made it stronger, but the core design is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee a few weeks later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Olav Sabo introduced the Income Equity Act of 1993 on October 13, 1993 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred jointly to the House Committees on Education and Labor and on Ways and Means on the day it was introduced [S3] [S5].
On November 3, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety in the Education and Labor Committee [S5].
Seven Democratic House members cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action appears in the record; the bill remained in subcommittee and expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage employers and corporations with very high executive pay are better off because the bill died — they avoided both a 53% higher wage floor and the loss of tax deductions on excessive compensation. Minimum-wage workers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Martin Olav Sabo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax provision
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the minimum wage provision
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent the bill to its Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety on November 3, 1993, and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, but no votes were ever taken, so the partisan split beyond sponsorship cannot be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, other minimum-wage industries)
industries.note: A $6.50 minimum wage would have raised their payroll costs significantly. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the wage gains it would have delivered to workers.

industries.industry: Corporations with very high executive compensation
industries.note: They would have lost the tax deduction on executive pay above 25 times their lowest worker's wages, meaning taxpayers would stop sharing the cost of extreme pay packages. The pay itself would still be allowed.
Ending the deduction for excessive compensation would have raised federal revenue by no longer subsidizing very high executive salaries through deductible business expenses.
